statement: In people taking opioids long-term who have constipation caused by them, mostly people with chronic non-cancer pain and some with cancer pain or after surgery (27 placebo-controlled randomized trials published to March 2017, 5390 people on a medicine and 3491 on placebo as printed, though the alvimopan figures do not add up, pooled in a meta-analysis read as its accepted manuscript), prescription medicines for opioid-induced constipation, compared with placebo, reduce the chance of not responding by each trial's definition (most often at least three complete spontaneous bowel movements a week): relative risk of failing to respond 0.70 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.75), with about 52 in 100 responding on a medicine against 33 in 100 on placebo (editors' calculation from the printed counts). The effect was smaller with the prescription laxative lubiprostone (0.90, 0.83 to 0.97) than with the medicines that block opioid receptors in the gut (methylnaltrexone, naloxone, naloxegol, naldemedine and alvimopan: 0.62 to 0.77 by drug), and it held in the trials at low risk of bias. Side effects were more common on the medicines: diarrhoea in about 9 against 5 in 100, abdominal pain in about 13 against 6 in 100, and about 7 against 5 in 100 stopped because of side effects. Results varied between trials and the funnel plot was asymmetric, so the size of the benefit may be overstated. Nearly all the trials were in people taking opioids for pain; one also enrolled people dependent on opioids, and a trial in methadone maintenance was set aside as an outlier, so the results say little about people using heroin or on methadone or buprenorphine treatment. No included trial tested over-the-counter laxatives. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
plain: In 27 trials of people taking opioids for pain, prescription medicines for opioid constipation helped more people go to the toilet normally than a dummy pill did (about 52 against 33 in 100), but caused more diarrhoea and tummy pain. None of the trials was in people using heroin or on methadone or buprenorphine treatment.
population: People taking opioids long-term with opioid-induced constipation, mostly for chronic non-cancer pain, some with cancer pain or advanced illness or after orthopaedic surgery (27 randomized trials)
exposure: Prescription medicines for opioid-induced constipation: peripherally acting opioid-receptor blockers (methylnaltrexone, naloxone, naloxegol, naldemedine, alvimopan, axelopran) and the prescription laxatives lubiprostone and prucalopride
outcome: Failure to respond by each trial's definition (most often fewer than three complete spontaneous bowel movements a week); adverse events and dropout for adverse events
magnitude: RR of failure to respond 0.70 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.75), 27 trials, 8881 participants, I2 77.9%; FDA-approved drugs 0.69 (0.62 to 0.77), NNT 5 (4 to 7). Response 2784 of 5390 (51.7%, editors' calculation; printed 51.3%) against 1157 of 3491 (33.1%). By drug: methylnaltrexone 0.62 (cancer-related pain 0.51, 0.41 to 0.63; non-cancer 0.75, 0.63 to 0.90), naloxone 0.63 (0.56 to 0.71), naldemedine 0.65 (0.52 to 0.82), alvimopan 0.68 (0.58 to 0.80), naloxegol 0.77 (0.61 to 0.97), lubiprostone 0.90 (0.83 to 0.97). Low-risk trials 0.67 (0.58 to 0.78). Adverse events: any 58.2% against 53.0% (RR 1.10, 1.05 to 1.16); diarrhoea 8.5% against 4.7%; abdominal pain 12.8% against 5.5%; nausea or vomiting 11.5% against 10.1%; dropout for adverse events 7.4% against 4.7%, NNH 36 (22 to 96).

risk_of_bias.note: Trials at low risk of bias gave the same estimate as the rest (0.67 against 0.71); several trials are known only from abstracts, and the review rated only naloxone down. The review itself is AMSTAR 2 critically low (card sc_nee_2018), which bears mainly on the size of the benefit, taken up under publication bias.

inconsistency.note: I2 77.9% across eight drugs, but 23 of 27 trials favour the medicine with intervals excluding no effect (forest plot, PDF p. 38) and much of the spread follows the drug, cancer pain and laxative history; the claim gives the range by drug.

indirectness.note: Worded for people taking opioids long-term, mostly for pain. For people using heroin or on methadone or buprenorphine treatment the evidence is indirect, as the statement says.

publication_bias.note: Egger's test significant with and without the outlier (Z = -5.06 and -4.79); not reflected in the review's GRADE; the benefit may be inflated.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; publication bias -1 gives moderate. The direction of benefit is consistent and holds in low-risk trials; its size is less certain because of small-study effects and several reporting errors in the review (alvimopan totals, side-effect ratios; card sc_nee_2018), which is why the side effects are given here as the printed proportions. Status replicated: 27 trials from many research groups point the same way; the earlier meta-analysis by Ford et al. (2013) shares most trials and is not counted separately.

statement: In people with constipation caused by opioids, evidence from the sources read is insufficient to say whether over-the-counter laxatives, compared with placebo or with prescription medicines, relieve it: a meta-analysis of 27 placebo-controlled trials of prescription medicines (searched to March 2017) included no trial of an over-the-counter laxative, and its authors write that such laxatives are often tried first, that their effect in opioid-induced constipation is hard to assess from existing studies because of varied methods, missing data and risk of bias (citing two Cochrane reviews of laxatives in palliative care, not read for this claim), and that prescription laxatives may not be better than over-the-counter ones. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: The review we read did not test laxatives that you can buy without a prescription, so we cannot yet say how well they work for constipation caused by opioids. Its authors say the older studies of these laxatives are hard to judge.
population: People with opioid-induced constipation (the review's trials were mostly in people taking opioids for chronic pain)
comparator: Placebo, or prescription medicines for opioid-induced constipation
magnitude: No data in the review read: no over-the-counter laxative trial was included. The authors' remark that their effect is hard to assess cites two Cochrane reviews in palliative care (Candy et al. 2011 and 2015), not read.

risk_of_bias.note: Not rated: there are no outcome data on the question.

indirectness.note: The only statement on the question is the review authors' second-hand remark about reviews in palliative care.

grade.reasoning: The question matters in real life (ordinary laxatives are what most people try first), but the sources read hold no data on it: the meta-analysis did not include such laxatives, and its authors' remark is second-hand. Starting low because no randomized evidence on the question was read; indirectness -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. The Cochrane review the authors cite (Candy et al. 2015, doi:10.1002/14651858.CD003448.pub4) is the source to read next.
